title: Inline photoluminescence maps each tier's defects before stacking the next
idea: Effect: photoluminescence (band-edge versus defect-band emission). In monolithic 3D DRAM, after each crystalline tier forms, a wafer-scale PL scan maps trap density per subarray region; the map goes into a per-die non-volatile sparing table so defective tier regions are logically spared, and the process tool receives feedback for the next wafer.
why: 10x density: 50 tiers at 99% yield each is only 60% stack yield, which kills cost parity; PL-driven region sparing lifts effective yield above 90%, making a ~50-tier (~10x) stack cost-competitive.

title: Bubble memory's bias-magnet killer removed with zero-field skyrmion loops
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) never needed refresh but died because it required permanent bias magnets and coil drives, making it slow and bulky. Fix: use exchange-biased synthetic-antiferromagnet multilayers that stabilize skyrmions at zero applied field, move them with spin-orbit current around loops, and keep bubble memory's proven major/minor-loop redundancy with an on-chip bad-loop map.
why: Nonvolatile with zero refresh, built-in yield repair from loop sparing, and many bits per access transistor for density without a capacitor.

title: Grade-B DRAM exchange selling dies with certified error maps
idea: Box [medium: any | access: any | sense: standard | integration: DIMM or CXL | substrate: bulk | fab: existing fabs]. A broker buys dies that fail JEDEC retention or hammer limits, tests each to a signed per-die error map, and sells them to hyperscalers whose controllers load the map to retire rows and set per-bank refresh.
why: Supply: unlocks the 5-15% of output that is scrapped or downbinned today, at ~40% discount.

title: Silicon carbide access transistors erase the leakage tail
idea: Worse: use narrow-bandgap silicon whose thermal generation and band-to-band tunneling create the leakage tail. Flip: bond a thin SiC layer (Si, C) as the access-transistor tier above a Si periphery wafer; its ~3.2 eV bandgap suppresses junction and tunneling leakage by orders of magnitude.
why: Fact 3: retention could rise from milliseconds to minutes, removing most refresh energy and making large, leaky abundant-element capacitors acceptable.

title: Miner-style undervolting: per-bank array voltage servoed by live ECC counts
idea: Crypto miners undervolt memory until errors just begin to appear. Give each bank its own array-voltage regulator and a closed loop that lowers VARY in 10 mV steps while that bank's on-die ECC corrected-error rate stays under budget, and backs off immediately on a burst. Banks with strong cells may settle near 0.8 V instead of ~1.05 V.
why: Array CV^2 energy is pinned at the voltage floor (fact 10). Running each bank at its real margin saves ~25-35% of array and refresh energy, and lets parts with weaker banks still meet energy specs.

title: Defense-grade beachhead: large-cell rad-tolerant DRAM in US mature fabs
idea: Satellites, missiles and nuclear plants pay 10-100x per bit for radiation-tolerant memory. Build a 28-40 nm-class DRAM with large capacitors (~15-25 fF), on-die ECC and hammer-immune row spacing in an underused U.S. mature-node fab, funded by defense and space demand. Then move the same line and team toward commercial nodes.
why: Attacks U.S. manufacturability (1-2% world share) and capital intensity: no EUV, depreciated tools, and a high-margin reliability niche that pays for the learning curve (fact 4).

title: Wafer-position-aware ECC strength fused per die
idea: Scale jump (wafer map -> die config): edge and notch-region dies show worse retention tails, so at sort each die's ECC mode (SEC vs DEC vs chipkill-lite) is fused based on its wafer radius and measured margin. Strong dies ship more user capacity and weak dies ship more parity.
why: Turns marginal edge dies into sellable parts and reclaims ~3-6% capacity on center dies.

title: Discharge-slope telemetry from normal reads builds live retention map
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: time-to-digital sense amp | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: EUV]. Each sense amp records the picoseconds the bitline takes to cross a threshold, which encodes the cell's remaining charge; the controller turns these free samples from ordinary reads into a continuously updated per-row retention class and adapts each row's refresh period.
why: Fact 3: retention profiling with no test downtime that also catches variable-retention-time cells live; ~4x fewer refresh operations.

title: Exponential-decay bloom filter tracks hours-long VRT toggling
idea: Timescale shift (64 ms refresh -> hours-long trap dwell): variable-retention-time cells flip between leaky and good trap states with hours-scale dwell. The controller keeps a time-decaying counting bloom filter of rows that recently showed corrected errors and refreshes only those fast, letting entries fade as the dwell statistics expire.
why: Handles the VRT tail that static retention profiling misses, enabling relaxed baseline refresh (e.g. 256 ms) with near-zero escapes.

title: Telomerase anneal: on-die microheaters periodically reset leakage traps
idea: Embed polysilicon micro-heaters under each mat; in maintenance windows the mat's data is moved out and the mat is flash-annealed (~300 C for ~10 ms) to re-passivate the hydrogen-related interface traps and GIDL defects that create variable-retention and hammer-damaged cells, resetting the 'telomere' of the array.
why: Retention tail and aging (VRT cells force worst-case refresh): in-field healing could double to quadruple the refresh interval and extend part lifetime, letting weaker initial bins qualify.

title: Selectron holding-beam revival: global flood pulse re-latches every cell
idea: RCA's Selectron kept every bit stable with a flood of 'holding' electrons that pushed each eyelet to the nearer of two stable potentials. Give each storage node a weak bistable element (an ovonic threshold switch to a shared flood line plus a high-resistance leak) so one flood pulse every ~64 ms tops up every node still above threshold while discharged nodes stay low, restoring the whole array at once with no row activation and no bitline swing.
why: Refresh energy and bandwidth (facts 3, 9): replaces ~46 fJ/bit row-by-row refresh with one array-wide pulse (goal ~5x less energy), returns 10-20% of bandwidth and removes refresh activations that add to hammer stress.

title: State-dependent gate capacitance enables global read-free refresh pulse
idea: Gate capacitance differs 2-3x between inversion ('1') and depletion ('0'). A global ratchet pulse train on the read-transistor source couples more charge into '1' nodes than into '0' nodes, and the write device's subthreshold conduction acts as the rectifying pawl. Every row is then refreshed at once with no sensing.
why: Refresh (fact 3): no activates, no sense amps, no bandwidth loss. Energy approaches the leaked-charge minimum.

title: Sauna recovery: on-die micro-heaters anneal traps after data evacuation
idea: Blocks of the array embed TiN resistive heaters; monthly, a block is evacuated by row copy, heated to ~250 C for seconds to recover BTI and anneal interface traps, then returned to service.
why: Repeatedly resets the aging clock during 10 years at 125 C, holding leakage tail and SA offset near time-zero and removing ~20-30% end-of-life retention margin.

title: Imperfect-by-contract DRAM tier for noise-trained AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must be perfect': a DRAM tier runs with refresh stretched 8x (~512 ms) and a published raw BER (1e-7 to 1e-5); training frameworks inject bit-flip noise matched to that datasheet BER in the final epochs so models are certified robust, and the runtime places weights and KV-cache only on this tier.
why: Refresh energy/bandwidth (fact 3) cut ~85% on the tier; dies failing standard retention bins become sellable, raising effective supply ~10-15%.

title: Ge: germanium strike-detector diodes turn soft errors into cheap erasures
idea: A grid of SiGe particle-strike detector diodes under each mat timestamps and localizes ion strikes; the controller marks the affected symbols as erasures, and because a code corrects twice as many erasures as unknown errors, the same ECC budget covers double the failure density.
why: Keeps on-die ECC overhead low (~6% die) while tolerating smaller Cs and weaker cells; also guides targeted scrubbing.

title: Crossbar sneak paths decoded as signal via multi-bias network inversion
idea: Selector-less resistive crossbars (HP, Crossbar Inc.) died because sneak currents corrupt reads in large arrays. Fix: read each small tile under K pseudo-random bias patterns and solve the resistor-network inverse problem (belief propagation / least squares) for every cell conductance, treating sneak current as known mixing rather than noise.
why: Enables true 4F2 selector-free arrays with no selector material or mask, trading extra read energy for ~1.5x density and fewer process steps.

title: Unsupported ultra-tall pillars: let 1% lean and short
idea: Po: let the capacitors fall over. Capacitor pillars are etched to AR ~115:1 without nitride support-mesh layers; the ~1% that lean, bridge or collapse become stuck cells mapped as erasures.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): reaches the higher Cs needed for scaling without a new dielectric, and removes 2-4 mesh deposition/patterning steps.

title: Substitute zero-error spec with a JEDEC relaxed-BER memory grade
idea: Define a standard 'DDR-R/HBM-R' grade with a guaranteed raw BER (e.g., 1e-6) and mandatory host-side strong ECC, letting fabs sell high-BER dies into AI and cache tiers under a common spec and price.
why: Supply and cost per bit: unlocks downbinned output across all vendors and lets future nodes trade reliability for density (fact 4) ~10-20%.

title: Core-sorting bins: grade dry-process DRAM into tiers, sell every die
idea: Core-memory makers tested every ferrite core and sorted them into hysteresis grades for different products. A DRAM maker running an all-dry, water-lean fab tests each die for retention and defect class and sells three grades with their own pricing and warranties: server ECC, AI-tensor (relaxed retention handled by the controller) and edge (reduced capacity, soft-formatted).
why: Water and cost per bit: the dry flow's wider defect spread becomes a product mix instead of a yield loss, which pays for converting a fab to ~10x less ultrapure water; ~95% of dies sold instead of ~85%.

title: Farmer overplants then thins: printed spare columns plus printed WORM map
idea: A farmer sows extra seed and then thins it: gravure- or inkjet-printed oxide-TFT gain-cell arrays on foil carry ~40% spare columns; an in-line probe on the web tests each tile and writes its bad-column map into a printed write-once (electrochemical-fuse) ROM on the same foil, which the attached CMOS controller reads at boot.
why: Printed TFT device yield of 99-99.9% gives near-zero yield for Mb-scale arrays; redundancy plus an on-foil map raises array yield above 90%, the precondition for any printed memory tier.

title: Flash-as-DRAM endurance killer fixed by triple-barrier resonant-tunneling storage
idea: Attempts to use floating-gate flash as working memory died on tunnel-oxide wear (~1e5 cycles) and high write voltage. Fix: replace the oxide with an InAs/AlSb triple-barrier resonant-tunneling structure that is opaque at rest but passes electrons at a ~2.5 V resonance, so charge enters the floating gate without hot-carrier damage (UltraRAM-style).
why: Nonvolatile, zero refresh, low-voltage writes with reported >1e7 cycles; a capacitor-free 1T cell with a path toward DRAM-class endurance.

title: Refresh doubles as scrub via per-subarray syndrome engines
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: a small shared syndrome/correct engine on each subarray sense-amp stripe checks every row while it sits in the sense amps during its refresh activation and writes corrected bits back before precharge.
why: Every row is scrubbed every refresh window (vs DDR5 ECS ~once per 24 h, >1000x more often), so single-bit errors never accumulate into uncorrectable doubles; tolerates ~100x weaker cells for ~2-3% area.

title: Stretch refresh until the raw error rate reaches 1%
idea: Po: memory that never refreshes on time. With 1% BER tolerated, the refresh window is set at the 1% quantile of the retention distribution (typically seconds) instead of the 64 ms dictated by the 1e-9 tail, and every refresh passes through the decoder as a scrub.
why: Refresh (fact 3): ~10-30x fewer refreshes, recovering 10-20% bandwidth and 15-30% of idle power at 32-64 Gb densities.

title: Cray-2 Fluorinert revival: boiling-pinned memory retunes refresh without water
idea: The Cray-2 (1985) ran its stacked boards submerged in circulating Fluorinert. Immerse DIMMs and HBM in a low-GWP two-phase fluid boiling at ~50 C, which pins every die at that temperature, then calibrate refresh interval, sense trims and ECC strength once for 50 C instead of the 85-95 C worst case; vapour is condensed by dry coolers.
why: Water and refresh (fact 3): dry condensers need no evaporative towers (WUE ~1.8 to <0.1 L/kWh, >10x), and a pinned 50 C die leaks ~8x less than at 85 C, so refresh falls ~4-8x and the retention tail stops limiting weaker cells.

title: Gold and bronze subarrays split AI words by bit significance
idea: Worse: protect a weight's least-significant mantissa bit as fiercely as its sign and exponent. Flip: transpose bfloat16/FP8 words into bit planes; store sign+exponent in a 'gold' subarray (64 ms refresh, ECC) and low mantissa bits in a 'bronze' subarray refreshed every 1-2 s with no ECC, where rare flips cost <0.01% accuracy.
why: Facts 3 and 7: ~60% of AI bits move to relaxed refresh with no parity, cutting refresh power ~50% and ECC area for AI-dominated capacity.

title: Substitute in-place NV writes with ping-pong shadow-row versioning
idea: Map each logical row to two physical NV rows and write updates alternately with a version and CRC, so a write cut by power loss leaves the old row valid and wear is spread across both copies.
why: Power-fail atomicity with no logging software and 2x wear spreading; doubles endurance of FeRAM/ReRAM-class cells at 2x raw bits for hot regions only.

title: Refresh-by-relocation: every refresh moves data to a new row
idea: Po: data runs away from the hammer. Instead of restoring a row in place, refresh copies it (RowClone-style, inside the subarray) to a free spare row and updates a small in-DRAM indirection table, so each logical row wanders across physical rows every window and no victim keeps the same neighbors for long.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): an aggressor's disturbance is spread over many short-lived residents; effective threshold x8-16 with ~1-2% spare rows.

title: Adaptive-optics guide-star canary cells in every subarray
idea: Adaptive optics measures the atmosphere with a bright guide star. Each subarray holds about 64 deliberately weakened canary cells (smaller cap, closer spacing) that fail at ~1/2 the retention time and ~1/2 the hammer count of normal cells. A comparator scan during refresh catches canary flips and locally doubles refresh or restores the neighbours.
why: Nominal refresh can then be set for typical conditions while canaries give in-situ early warning. That cuts refresh 40-60% (fact 3) and adds a hammer tripwire (fact 9).

title: Farmer's seed bank: OS donates pages as a growing spare-row pool
idea: A farmer keeps a seed bank instead of a fixed spare field: the memory controller's small CAM remaps failing lines found in the field into a pool of pages the OS donates (0.1-0.5% of capacity), and the pool grows as the module ages instead of relying only on the fixed spare rows fused at the factory.
why: Lets fabs ship dies with fewer on-die spares and lets weaker cells survive field aging; cuts scrap and DIMM RMAs.

title: Fine-tune each model to its own DRAM's fault map
idea: Reverse adaptation: instead of repairing memory to fit the model, each deployed model is briefly fine-tuned with weights forced to zero at the exact stuck or weak bit positions of the DRAM it occupies, absorbing the higher defect density of a fluorine-free fab.
why: Ships dies with ~1e-5 hard-fault density for inference at <0.1% accuracy loss and no repair area.

title: Adaptive twin-cell fusion of weak row pairs as cells age
idea: Time shift (static 1T1C -> on-the-fly 2T2C): when a row pair shows weak retention, the controller reconfigures them into a differential twin-cell pair (true and complement stored), halving that pair's capacity but doubling signal and cancelling common-mode leakage.
why: Rescues the weakest ~0.1-1% of rows at 2x local cost instead of discarding the die; a graceful-degradation path for aging.

title: Wolff's-law remodeling: hot rows migrate into guard-flanked bunkers
idea: Bone reinforces where it is loaded; keep a small pool of 'bunker' rows in each bank that are physically flanked by unused guard rows, and when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold the controller swaps it into a bunker, where hammering has no victims.
why: Row hammer: guarantees zero victims for the hottest rows at ~1-2% capacity cost instead of victim-refresh overhead that explodes as thresholds approach 1k.

title: RAID-5 across HBM stacks accepts one dead die
idea: Inverts 'every die in a stack must work': the accelerator controller stripes each line across 8 HBM stacks with one parity channel, so a stack with one failed core die or channel ships and runs degraded instead of being scrapped.
why: HBM stacked-yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6) could fall by more than half; parity costs ~12% capacity but saves whole stacks.

title: Partial-good HBM: channel-isolated stacks sold and run degraded
idea: Rule: a dead channel must not kill a stack. Each HBM pseudo-channel gets independent power gating and fuse-isolatable TSV groups, so stacks with failed channels ship as 75% or 50% capacity SKUs, and channels that fail in the field are fenced off instead of retiring the stack.
why: Fact 6: recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss as sellable bits and lengthens field life.

title: Recombination-sink grid absorbs hammer electrons at much tighter pitch
idea: Effect: minority-carrier recombination in engineered short-lifetime silicon. A self-aligned buried carbon-doped or p+ grid runs between adjacent active rows; electrons injected by aggressor activation recombine inside this short-lifetime strip before reaching victim nodes, while storage junctions stay in long-lifetime silicon.
why: 10x density: tighter rows would otherwise drop hammer thresholds below ~100 and mitigation refresh would erase the gain; the sink allows ~40% row and tier pitch shrink, which with 16-tier stacking gives ~10x at the cost of one implant or epi step.

title: Mg: polymerase-style proofreading verifies writes before row close
idea: Like DNA polymerase's Mg2+-dependent proofreading, controller RTL reads back freshly written columns before precharge while the row is still open and checks ECC; a mismatch triggers a rewrite with longer tWR or a remap.
why: Write-recovery failures grow as Cs shrinks (fact 1); verifying catches them before they become latent errors and allows aggressive tWR safely.

title: Early FeRAM imprint fix revived: periodic polarity flips cancel sense-amp aging
idea: Early FeRAMs fought imprint, where a cell held in one state too long comes to prefer it, and periodic inverted rewriting was a classic remedy. DRAM sense-amp latches age asymmetrically (BTI drift) when data sit unchanged for months at high temperature, so every N refresh epochs each row is rewritten inverted under a per-row polarity bit and both latch halves age equally.
why: Water: sense-amp offset drift is a key barrier to 105-115 C operation over 5+ years; cancelling it lets memory run hot enough for dry coolers (>10x less water) while keeping sense margin for weak cells (fact 1).

title: Slew-shaped wordline pulses cut hammer coupling
idea: No EUV: drive wordlines with controlled 2-5 ns ramps and an early-close discharge profile instead of sharp sub-ns edges, reducing capacitive coupling and hot-electron injection into victim nodes. Timescale shift: the change is in ps-to-ns edge physics, not geometry.
why: Could raise hammer thresholds ~2-5x at no lithography cost, at a small tRAS penalty.

title: Soft-decision sensing plus NAND LDPC to read tiny capacitors
idea: Combine the DRAM sense amp with NAND flash soft-read: the bitline is compared against 3-7 shifted references (a mini flash-ADC sharing one regenerative latch) to give per-bit confidence, and a short-latency LDPC decoder at the bank uses those log-likelihoods. Cells with roughly half today's charge (~2.5 fF, AR ~35) then read at acceptable error rates.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): halving required Cs cuts capacitor aspect ratio ~2x, saving etch/deposition steps and easing 3D tiers; costs ~6-10% parity and a few ns.

title: Lumber-grade radial zones: extra redundancy designed into wafer-edge fields
idea: Sawmills grade heartwood and sapwood differently; when helium backside cooling is replaced by electrostatic chucks with hydrogen or conductive-elastomer contact, accept wider centre-to-edge CD drift and print two reticle designs, full-density centre fields and edge-ring fields with 2x spare rows/columns and stronger on-die ECC.
why: Makes helium-free thermal control yield-neutral by spending redundancy only where non-uniformity lives, keeping ~90-95% of the wafer at full density.

title: Lattice-defect-aware codes for self-assembled cell arrays
idea: Block-copolymer self-assembly makes near-perfect hexagonal arrays whose defects are known topological types (dislocations, disclinations, grain boundaries) that displace lines or wedges of cells; design hexagonal-lattice codes whose syndromes recognise exactly those fault shapes, so DSA-patterned arrays with ~1e-4 defect density stay usable.
why: Lets self-assembly replace several EUV/ArF patterning passes (fact 4: 5-7 EUV layers) by making its intrinsic defectivity acceptable through matched decoding.

title: Sense-settling timer flags marginal bits as erasures
idea: Ideal: knowing exactly which bits are wrong without storing extra bits. Closest: a per-column comparator times how long each sense amp takes to resolve; bits that resolve slowly (small signal) are flagged to the decoder as erasures, and since an erasure costs half an error, a code fixing t errors now fixes 2t marginal bits.
why: Facts 1 and 3: doubles effective ECC strength at no parity cost, allowing ~2x weaker cells or 2-4x longer refresh.

title: Sous-vide chilled DRAM using absorption chillers, not cryogens
idea: Sous vide holds food at an exact temperature; hold memory modules at a precise 5-10C with waste-heat-driven lithium-bromide/water absorption chillers (no helium cryogenics) and program refresh from measured temperature, since retention roughly doubles per 10C drop.
why: Refresh can relax ~8x versus 85C, cutting refresh power and bandwidth (fact 3) by ~85% and letting weak tail cells pass, powered by data-centre waste heat.

title: Minify leakage by decades with SiC-substrate wide-bandgap access transistors
idea: Build the 1T1C access device as a 4H-SiC MOSFET on SiC substrates, with capacitors deposited above. SiC's intrinsic carrier density is ~1e-8 cm^-3 versus ~1e10 in Si, so junction and band-to-band leakage almost disappear.
why: Fact 3: retention could reach hours at 85C, making refresh nearly vanish, and the U.S. has domestic SiC substrate capacity. SiC/SiO2 interface traps and mobility are the risks.

title: Substitute refresh for retention-noise-aware model training on mantissa planes
idea: Store AI weights bit-sliced so sign/exponent bits sit in normally refreshed rows and low mantissa bits sit in never-refreshed 'leaky planes'; models are fine-tuned with injected DRAM-decay noise matching measured retention statistics so accuracy holds with mantissa bits decaying.
why: Refresh energy and density (facts 1,3): ~50% of weight bits need no refresh and can use cheaper, smaller-capacitor cells, cutting effective cost per weight-bit ~25-35%.

title: Sell capacity-years: DIMMs that shrink gracefully as rows retire
idea: Time shift (time-zero spec -> lifetime contract): ship modules with weaker cells that the OS retires row by row as they degrade, and price them per guaranteed GB-year with a declining capacity curve (e.g. 100% -> 92% over 5 years). Today those weaker cells are screened out at the factory.
why: Lets fabs sell lower retention bins (an estimated 5-15% more good bits per wafer) and moves reliability from screening to contract.

title: KV-cache precision decays with token age in leaky cells
idea: Time shift (data age = allowed precision): store the LSBs of older KV-cache tokens in unrefreshed weak cells and their MSBs in refreshed cells, so old context loses precision over seconds the way attention already discounts it. New tokens get full refresh.
why: Removes refresh for ~40-60% of KV bits and allows lower-grade cells for long-context inference memory.

title: Dynamic guard rows flank hot aggressors by migrating neighbors
idea: Scale/time shift (fixed layout -> runtime layout): when a row's activation rate crosses a threshold within a refresh window, the controller migrates its two physical neighbors' data elsewhere so the hot row is temporarily flanked by empty guard rows; the rows are re-filled when it cools.
why: Neutralizes hammer for the hot set at near-zero refresh cost, tolerating thresholds below 1k without per-row victim refresh storms.

title: Hammer-immune coarse-pitch DUV memory sold as secure tier
idea: No EUV: hammer thresholds rise steeply with wordline pitch, so 25-30 nm-class DUV DRAM has thresholds of ~50k+ activations. Scale/time shift (old node reframed as security feature): market it as a premium hammer-immune tier for multi-tenant clouds and confidential computing.
why: Gives new US DUV fabs a profitable segment where the reliability gain pays for the density loss.

title: Revive depreciated 2010s DUV DRAM lines with weak-die-accepting ECC
idea: No EUV: buy or restart fully depreciated 30-40 nm DUV DRAM fabs whose capital cost is already written off, and ship their output with stronger on-module ECC and runtime row retirement so higher defect and retention-fail rates still meet spec. Time shift: a decade-old asset meets 2026 demand.
why: Depreciation is ~55% of leading-edge wafer cost, so these bits could be ~40-50% cheaper per wafer despite lower density; also usable for U.S. capacity.

title: ECC compresses the yield-learning curve from years to months
idea: No EUV: a new DUV DRAM line normally needs 18-24 months of yield learning before it can ship. Time shift: ship from month 3 with heavy on-die ECC plus OS row retirement covering immature defect density, then relax ECC by firmware as the line matures.
why: Brings new fab revenue and supply forward by about a year, which matters more than density during a 4x price spike.

title: Year-two DIMM remanufacturing: re-profile, re-fuse, resell
idea: No EUV: take back modules at year two, re-test them with fleet telemetry, re-fuse repairs and retire weak ranks, then resell them with a refreshed warranty. Time shift: product life runs past 5 years and needs no new wafers.
why: Stretches existing bit supply by ~30-50% of lifetime output with zero fab capex during the shortage.

title: Floppy soft-sectoring revival: per-region code strength formats dry-cleaned dies
idea: Soft-sectored floppies were formatted after manufacture around their actual media defects. After wafer test, firmware formats each subarray with an ECC strength chosen from its measured defect density (none, SECDED, BCH-4 or retire) and records it in a die format table, so the clustered, edge-heavy particle defects of an all-dry clean flow (cryogenic aerosol, radical plasma, vapour HF) cost a few percent of capacity instead of whole dies.
why: Water: wet cleans and rinses are ~70-80% of a DRAM fab's ultrapure water; an all-dry flow plus air-cooled chillers is a ~10x water cut, and soft formatting absorbs its ~3-5x higher particle defectivity at roughly flat cost per bit.

title: Refresh that shifts every row one slot, dissolving neighbors
idea: Inverts 'a row's physical neighbors are fixed': each refresh pass copies row i into row i+1 with in-subarray copy instead of restoring in place, then bumps a per-subarray offset register, so logical rows migrate continuously and no aggressor stays beside the same victim for more than one window.
why: Defeats targeted row hammer (fact 9) and spreads disturb at near-zero cost, since refresh already reads and rewrites every row.

title: Chaos-engineering controller that probes margins with shadow writes
idea: Inverts 'operate safely inside a fixed guardband': the controller continuously writes shadow copies of live lines into a scratch row using aggressive timings and refresh, compares them with the protected original, and learns per-bank safe tRCD/tRAS/refresh envelopes that track temperature and aging.
why: Recovers the 20-40% timing and refresh guardband sized for worst-case cells (facts 3, 10), raising usable bandwidth and lowering energy.

title: Random nanowire crossbars addressed by post-fab calibrated stochastic decoder
idea: Effect: stochastic self-assembly. Sub-10 nm-pitch Si nanowire crossbars are grown or transfer-printed with gain cells at the crossings and no litho at cell scale; each wire carries a randomly doped code region, a post-fab discovery pass learns which address code activates which wire and stores a translation table, and defective wires are simply never mapped.
why: 10x density: 4F^2 crossbars at F ~5 nm without EUV give >10x bits/mm^2. Same cost: error tolerance turns disorder into a feature, so no precision patterning is paid for.

title: Flash-style detrap pulses heal variable-retention-time cells in field
idea: Combine NAND erase-style detrapping with DRAM self-refresh: during idle, access transistors get brief negative-gate and reverse-junction bias pulses that empty the oxide/junction traps behind random-telegraph leakage, pushing VRT cells back into their low-leak state.
why: Leakage tail <=13 fA (fact 3): VRT cells force pessimistic refresh; pinning them low-leak could allow ~2x longer refresh and fewer field failures.

title: Spare-free dies: host controller owns all row repair
idea: Reverse who owns redundancy: DRAM dies carry no spare rows, fuse banks or address comparators; failing rows found at test go into a signed manifest and the host memory controller remaps them through an on-SoC 64 KB CAM into a host-reserved pool, one remap fabric serving dozens of dies.
why: Periphery is ~49% of die: removes ~3-5% die area of redundancy/fuses plus fuse-blow test time; yield loss becomes a small capacity haircut.

title: Codon-degeneracy encoding: likely bit-flips map to near-identical values
idea: The genetic code is arranged so most point mutations yield the same or a similar amino acid; encode AI weights and activations in a learned number format whose least-significant code bits are placed in each row's measured weakest cell positions and whose code assignment is Gray-like, so the most probable flips cause the smallest numerical change.
why: ECC and refresh cost for tolerant data (most AI memory): such regions can drop the 12.5% ECC overhead and run ~10x longer refresh with negligible accuracy loss.

title: N: nitride charge-trap sliver as per-row analog hammer dosimeter
idea: A thin SiN charge-trap strip (SONOS-like) under a dummy gate coupled to each wordline receives a small, repeatable charge injection on every activation, so its Vt shift integrates activation count non-volatilely; refresh logic compares it to a threshold, refreshes the neighbors and erases the strip.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) tracking with no SRAM/CAM counter tables, so per-row tracking at ~1k-activation thresholds costs almost no periphery (fact 7).

title: Spider web: dual-end wordline drive tolerates mid-line opens
idea: Each wordline segment is driven from both ends, with a weak keeper at the far end, so a single open (void, CMP break) still leaves both halves driven - a web that holds after one strand snaps; only shorts consume spare rows.
why: Opens are a large share of row repairs; ~30-50% fewer spare rows needed, returning array area and raising yield.

title: Sacrificial-anode collector implants absorb hammer-injected electrons
idea: Galvanising protects steel with a zinc anode that corrodes first; add a shallow grounded n+ collector ribbon (or biased deep well) between adjacent active regions in the buried-channel array so electrons emitted by aggressor wordline traps and passing-gate charge pumping are collected before they reach a victim storage node.
why: Attacks a physical root cause of row hammer (fact 9), possibly raising the threshold 5-20x and removing counter and refresh overhead at a modest density cost.

title: Self-repairing TSV mesh with spare vias and in-stack switches
idea: Rule: interconnect failures must heal in the field. Stacks include ~10% spare TSVs plus tiny per-die crossbar switches. In-field BIST detects TSVs degrading from electromigration or cracking and reroutes their signals to spares without removing the stack.
why: Fact 6: lowers stack yield loss and field returns from TSV defects, extending stack life.

title: Eliminate discard-on-error policy: re-harvest retired fleet DIMMs die-by-die
idea: An e-waste and procurement rule requires that DIMMs hyperscalers retire at correctable-error thresholds be offered to a re-test line before shredding. The line re-characterizes each die, maps its faults and repackages the healthy dies (the majority) into remapped modules for tolerant workloads.
why: Turns part of the millions of DIMMs retired each year into new supply with no wafer starts; immediate shortage relief.

title: V(D)J clonal selection: wire random nanowire meshes, then select working cells
idea: The immune system generates random receptors and keeps the ones that work; spray self-assembled nanowire/nanotube networks over a coarse CMOS grid with no fine lithography, probe at test time which random junctions behave as good storage cells, and record their addresses in an on-chip translation table, discarding the rest.
why: Capital/EUV: eliminates fine patterning of the array (5-7 EUV layers, ~55% depreciation share); even at 30% junction yield plus table overhead, cost per GB could fall ~100x because the array costs almost nothing to form.

title: Ant pheromone: analog decaying charge counters track row activations
idea: Each ACT deposits a fixed charge packet on a tiny per-row 'pheromone' capacitor beside the wordline driver; it leaks with a designed time constant near tREFW and a comparator fires a neighbor refresh at threshold, so the trail's evaporation is the sliding window for free.
why: Fact 9 (flips at ~1k ACTs): exact per-row tracking for ~2 transistors + 1 cap per row, <0.3% area versus 1-3% for SRAM/CAM counters.

title: Library LOCKSS: peer GPU replicas serve as ECC for weights
idea: Adapted from digital-preservation networks ('Lots Of Copies Keep Stuff Safe') that repair a corrupted copy from peers: in data-parallel inference and training, weights are already replicated on many GPUs, so HBM weight regions run detection-only parity with ECC disabled, and a detected error triggers a 64 B fetch of the same address from a peer GPU's replica over NVLink or Ethernet.
why: HBM capacity and cost (facts 5, 6): reclaims ~12.5% ECC capacity and sideband bandwidth for weight regions and lets lower-grade HBM stacks be used, with firmware and runtime changes only.

title: Optane endurance shielded by MMU write-budget traps and page migration
idea: 3D XPoint never displaced DRAM partly because ~1e7-1e8-cycle media wore out under hot writes. Fix: the MMU keeps a per-page write-budget counter, and a page exceeding its budget traps and migrates to a small SRAM-backed write log, so only read-mostly data (weights, code, indexes) ever lives in the nonvolatile tier.
why: Zero refresh for the bulk tier (read-mostly data is often >70% of AI-server bytes) with a guaranteed 5-year wear life; cuts DRAM bits needed.

title: Ti: titanium getter ring in hybrid-bond seal absorbs moisture
idea: Pattern a Ti/Zr getter line inside the hybrid-bonding seal ring of each stacked DRAM die so moisture and stray hydrogen entering through dicing edges are chemisorbed before reaching TSV liners and capacitor dielectrics.
why: Prevents time-dependent leakage drift and TSV corrosion in stacks, lifting HBM yield and field life (fact 6) with an abundant, MEMS-proven getter.

title: Substitute voltage-level sensing with time-to-threshold soft readout
idea: Replace the latch-type sense amp decision with a bitline discharge timer: the time for the bitline to cross a reference is digitized to 3 bits, giving soft reliability info per cell that a soft-decision LDPC decoder uses to fix marginal cells hard-decision ECC cannot.
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): soft decoding gains ~2-3 dB, which allows ~30-40% less stored charge per cell or longer refresh intervals.

title: Geiger ratemeter diode pump: one extra cell integrates row activations
idea: 1950s Geiger-counter ratemeters used a diode pump that added a fixed charge packet per pulse to a leaky capacitor, giving a time-windowed count with no logic. Each row gets one extra 'hammer cell' that receives a fixed charge quantum through a diode-connected device whenever its wordline fires, while natural leakage drains it; at refresh, a threshold sense reveals rows activated more than ~500 times recently and triggers neighbour restores.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): windowed activation counting for one cell per row (~0.01% area) instead of SRAM or in-array counters, with no timing penalty.

title: Bad-cell-map grade: ship scattered-defect dies with fused bitmaps
idea: Ideal: no die is ever scrapped. Closest: dies failing JEDEC only because of scattered bad cells are sold as a new grade carrying a fused, compressed bad-cell map that the host reads at boot, retiring the affected 4 KB pages or placing error-tolerant tensors there.
why: Supply axis: recovers ~5-15% of wafer output now down-binned or scrapped, raising usable bits with zero new capex.

title: Center-tapped wordlines for chloride-precursor molybdenum fill
idea: Rearrange the wordline driver from the end to the middle: buried wordlines filled with Mo from MoO2Cl2 (replacing tungsten from WF6) are driven from a center tap, halving RC so far-end cells get a full restore within tRAS.
why: Under-restored far-end cells feed the retention tail; also removes WF6 and dependence on China-concentrated tungsten.

title: Substitute verified strong MRAM writes with sloppy writes plus BCH
idea: Write STT-MRAM at ~0.6x critical current with no write-verify, accepting ~1e-4 write error rate, and correct with BCH-6 per 512 bits; the smaller write current allows a ~40% smaller access transistor.
why: Energy per bit and density: ~3x lower write energy and ~25-35% smaller cell while staying non-volatile.

title: Reinsurance pool: rack-level CXL spare memory absorbing failing pages
idea: Reinsurers pool rare risks across many insurers. Each rack keeps a shared CXL-attached spare pool of about 2% of rack capacity. The hypervisor live-migrates pages from any DIMM whose correctable-error rate rises into the pool, so individual DIMMs ship with thinner margins and fewer on-die spare rows.
why: Pooled spares scale with sqrt(N) instead of N. That recovers ~3-5% of die area spent on redundancy and raises yield, so cost per bit falls.

title: Sail-reefing mode: elastic conversion to twin-cell under thermal stress
idea: Sailors reef sails when the wind is high. When die temperature exceeds 85 C or the error rate climbs, the OS can switch selected subarrays from 1T1C to 2T2C twin-cell mode: complementary data in paired cells with differential sensing. That halves capacity but doubles the signal and stretches retention about 4x. Memory hot-unplug absorbs the lost capacity.
why: This avoids the 2x refresh penalty at high temperature (fact 3) and lets nominal cells be built weaker, because they have a safe fallback mode.

title: Charge-minimizing inversion coding keeps bits in non-leaking state
idea: Only the charged state decays, so the error rate scales with the fraction of charged cells. A per-32-bit codebook flag (bus-invert style, aware of true/anti polarity) stores each chunk so that >=65% of cells sit in the discharged state.
why: Retention errors/refresh: exposure to tail failures roughly halved, which permits ~2x longer refresh with the same ECC, plus lower write energy.

title: Tea-kettle whistle: ECC error rate, not temperature, drives thermal throttling
idea: Per-bank on-die ECC correction counters feed the SoC power manager; when corrected-error rate crosses a budget, adjacent compute is throttled or cooling boosted, replacing fixed 85/95 C thresholds that assume worst-case cells.
why: Most parts survive 125 C with margin; closing the loop on the real failure signal removes conservative 2x refresh and throttling guard-bands while holding the 10-year error budget.

title: O: lambda-sensor loop tunes DDR5 PMIC voltages to error rate
idea: Like an engine O2 sensor trimming fuel, DIMM firmware closes a loop on corrected-error and hammer-alert rates and nudges the on-DIMM PMIC's VPP and VDD within spec, lowering VPP to reduce hammer susceptibility and raising it if retention errors climb.
why: Finds each module's reliable minimum-energy point, cutting wordline CV2 energy (fact 10) and hammer flips (fact 9) using existing I2C-programmable PMICs.

title: Artist's negative space: asymmetric Z-channel ECC for one-way charge leakage
idea: An artist reads the empty space as much as the ink: retention errors almost always go from charged to discharged, so the controller tracks true-cell/anti-cell polarity per row, maps data so every retention error is a one-way flip, and uses asymmetric (Z-channel) error-correcting codes that need far fewer parity bits than symmetric BCH for the same correction.
why: Facts 1 and 3: ~40% less parity for equal protection, or about twice the retention errors corrected for equal overhead, which lets cells run on thinner margins.

title: Eliminate static storage: data circulates as a regenerated delay line
idea: Use leaky, capacitor-light cells (~1 ms retention) and keep moving data from row to row with in-array copy (RowClone-style). Each hop re-senses and re-amplifies like a repeater, so a row holds data for only one circulation slot. Reads are timed to the slot or served from the ring head.
why: Removes the retention-tail requirement entirely (fact 3) and lets Cs drop several-fold (fact 1); copy energy replaces refresh, and the density gain comes from the smaller capacitor.

title: Fiber-Bragg distributed thermometry setting per-mat refresh rates
idea: Fiber Bragg gratings measure temperature every metre along a fiber. Tiny diode or ring-oscillator thermometers are placed in every mat, and each mat's refresh multiplier follows its own temperature: hot spots under an HBM base die or next to a GPU get 2x, cool mats get 1x. Today the whole die refreshes at its worst-case temperature.
why: Retention halves for every ~10 C, and HBM stacks carry 10-20 C gradients. Matching refresh to each mat's temperature cuts refresh 30-50% (facts 3 and 6).

title: Flip-bounded number formats make weight memory ECC-free
idea: Po: numbers that can't be badly wrong. Weights use a redundant signed-digit encoding in which no single bit carries more than ~1/16 of the value range (e.g., 10 bits for 8-bit precision), so 1% raw flips act as small additive noise that noise-aware training absorbs with no decoder.
why: Zero decode latency and ~25% encoding overhead (vs ECC plus refresh) for the weight-streaming bulk of inference memory, run on cheap 1%-BER cells with minimal refresh.

title: Magnify the cell 20x on display glass: 100 fF planar capacitors
idea: Use LTPO display lines (oxide-TFT cells plus LTPS CMOS periphery) on Gen-8.5 glass at ~1.5 um rules, with planar high-k MIM capacitors of ~100 fF, 20x a silicon DRAM cell. Sense margins become so wide that raw BER is negligible without ECC.
why: Facts 1 and 4: no capacitor wall and no EUV. Density comes from panel area (~5 m^2, roughly tens of GB per panel) on fabs that cost far less per m^2 than a DRAM fab.

title: Gated-diode self-restoring cell refreshed by one global pulse
idea: Ideal: every cell refreshes itself at once with no sensing. Closest: add a small transistor whose gate is the storage node, in series with a poly diode from a global pulse line; when the line pulses high, cells holding '1' turn the transistor on and top themselves up while '0' cells stay off, so the whole array refreshes in one pulse.
why: Fact 3: replaces row-by-row refresh (bandwidth loss, ~46 fJ/bit) with a global pulse of a few fJ/bit; buildable at 180 nm.

title: Large DUV cells store two bits each under Gray-coded LDPC
idea: No EUV: a 38 nm DUV-patterned cell can hold ~2-3x the charge of a 12 nm cell, so use four charge levels per cell (MLC DRAM) with Gray mapping and a row-level LDPC to absorb the level-tail errors. The retention budget is rescaled to 16 ms for the level spacing.
why: Recovers ~2x bits per cell to offset the coarser DUV pitch; a density step without EUV capex.

title: Anti-lock-brake pulsed row-open time cap against RowPress
idea: ABS pulses the brakes so the wheels never lock. The open-source FPGA controller caps continuous row-open time (tAggON) at ~200 ns. A row being held open for hits has its buffer copied to a controller-side row cache and is closed early. That defeats RowPress, which multiplies flips 10-100x when rows stay open long.
why: Keeps ACT-count-based protection valid without 10x over-provisioning mitigation (fact 9). It is a policy change demonstrable on DDR5 within budget.

title: Optane wear tail decoded as erasures to double Reed-Solomon power
idea: 3D XPoint carried heavy ECC and indirection latency to cover its wear-out tail. Fix: per-line write counters in out-of-band metadata plus a per-cell wear model flag near-dead bits, which are passed to the Reed-Solomon decoder as erasures, since an erasure costs one parity symbol instead of two.
why: Same parity covers ~2x more worn bits, giving 3-5x longer life or half the ECC overhead for any wear-limited DRAM substitute (cost per bit, endurance).

title: Merge-mask bridges landing pads into double-charge cells
idea: Inverts 'one cell, one capacitor': one added mask bridges pairs of adjacent storage-node landing pads in a designated region so two pillars act as one ~10 fF capacitor driven by two access transistors in parallel.
why: Creates a robust region (2x signal, ~4x retention, immune to single-pillar defects) for metadata and ECC parity, letting the rest of the die use cheaper, weaker cells.

title: Ferroelectric ZnMgO shadow parity protects rows during long refresh gaps
idea: Worse: lean on Hf-based ferroelectrics, or just refresh harder, to guard idle data. Flip: add a small nonvolatile parity array of wurtzite ferroelectric Zn1-xMgxO (all abundant) per bank holding XOR parity of each row group; when relaxed refresh lets a row decay, its data is rebuilt from parity, and parity is rewritten rarely so ferroelectric endurance is enough.
why: Fact 3: allows 4-10x longer refresh intervals in idle banks for ~3% area, with a Hf-free ferroelectric.

title: Sense-amp resolution time as soft-decision reliability information
idea: TRIZ #13 The other way around: instead of waiting for bits to fail, each sense amp's latch time is compared with a delayed strobe; slow-resolving (low-margin) bits are flagged as soft erasures to the ECC decoder and queued for migration.
why: Soft-decision decoding gives ~2x correction or ~10x lower uncorrectable rate from the same parity and finds weak cells before they flip, letting refresh stretch ~2x.

title: Vertical XOR parity tier rescues defective layers in 3D DRAM
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: in a monolithic 3D DRAM with N tiers, one tier per vertical string stores XOR parity of the bits above it, so a whole failed tier, string segment or leaky-tier tail can be rebuilt by reading the column.
why: Fact 2: tier yield compounds (0.98^26 = 59%); tolerating one bad tier per string lifts yield to ~90% and makes 26+ tier break-even reachable with weaker lateral transistors.

title: Scratched-CD codes: cross-interleaved 2D product codes over each mat
idea: Car CD players survived scratches through CIRC, two Reed-Solomon codes crossed by interleaving. Apply a row-by-column product code over each 512x512 mat, so a whole failed wordline or bitline (a burst) is corrected by the orthogonal code during scrub instead of needing a fused spare.
why: Wordline and bitline defects and hammer clusters use up repair resources and yield. A 2D code corrects whole-line failures for ~6% overhead, cutting redundancy area and raising yield (facts 7, 9).

title: Tail exile: weak cells banished to an SRAM patch
idea: Ideal: a DRAM that never refreshes. Closest: a power-on BIST at elevated wordline-off stress finds the ~0.1% of cells with retention <2 s and stores their addresses in an on-die CAM plus a small SRAM patch that shadows those bits; the other 99.9% of the array is refreshed every 2-4 s instead of every 32-64 ms.
why: Fact 3 (leakage tail forces refresh): refresh energy and refresh bandwidth loss cut ~30-60x for the bulk array at ~0.5% area for the patch; VRT cells handled by periodic re-profiling.

title: Election risk-limiting audits replace exhaustive retention testing
idea: Adapted from risk-limiting election audits that certify a result by sampling ballots until statistical confidence is reached: wafer retention test samples random rows per mat with a sequential probability ratio test, stops early on clearly good mats, and escalates to a full retention sweep only for mats whose samples look risky; residual uncertainty is covered by in-field ECC.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): long retention and pattern tests tie up expensive testers for minutes per die; sequential sampling could cut test time 3-5x, freeing tester capital and raising throughput.

title: Eliminate module replacement: embedded microheaters anneal leaky cells in-situ
idea: Put thin resistive heater lines under each bank. In a maintenance window, the bank's data is migrated away and the bank is heated to ~250-300 C for seconds to anneal the interface traps and hot-carrier damage behind VRT and leakage tails, then the data is restored.
why: Self-heals the retention tail (fact 3), returning aged parts to near-fresh refresh needs; extends fleet life and permits longer refresh intervals.

title: Field-patchable row-hammer defense in an embedded FPGA buffer
idea: Rule: a new attack must never force a recall. Row-hammer mitigation runs in a small eFPGA or microcode engine in the RCD/CXL buffer, so new defenses against new attack variants can be patched over the air instead of discarding vulnerable modules.
why: Fact 9: avoids fleet-wide module replacement when thresholds drop or new attacks appear, keeping deployed DRAM in service.

title: Write first, compute on-die parity later in idle
idea: Reverse write ordering for on-die ECC: partial writes land immediately without read-modify-write, affected codewords are marked parity-stale in a small SRAM bitmap, and parity is recomputed at the next activation or idle slot, accepting a microsecond-scale unprotected window.
why: On-die ECC read-modify-write costs DDR5 up to ~10-20% write bandwidth; this recovers it while keeping protection for data at rest.

title: Library late fees: refresh debt budgeted against ECC correction margin
idea: Rows accrue a 'fine' equal to predicted bit-error probability (temperature, elapsed time, profiled retention class); the controller refreshes a row only when expected errors in its codewords approach a set fraction of the code's correction capacity, so healthy rows run overdue for seconds.
why: Fact 3: converts idle ECC slack into skipped refreshes, ~50-80% refresh reduction at <=1e-15 uncorrectable rate.

title: First-week in-field self-profiling replaces factory retention bakes
idea: No EUV: skip the hours-long high-temperature retention test at the factory. Time/scale shift (factory hours -> field week): the module ships with conservative refresh, self-profiles each row's retention during its first week in a server, then relaxes refresh row by row.
why: Cuts test capex and floor time (a major cost for mature-node fabs) and finds VRT/temperature-specific tails in their real environment.

title: Leaky-capacitor integrators count hammer activations automatically
idea: Ideal: hammer counting that needs no counter memory. Closest: a 180 nm companion chip holds an array of MOS capacitors, one per row group, each receiving a fixed charge packet per ACT and leaking with a time constant equal to the refresh window, so each voltage is a free sliding-window activation count; a comparator fires neighbor refresh at threshold.
why: Fact 9: analog decay implements the sliding window that digital trackers spend kilobytes of SRAM on; ~10x less area than counter tables.

title: Garbage-collector compaction doubles as hardware refresh
idea: Timescale coupling (ms GC cycles <-> 64 ms refresh): managed runtimes rewrite live objects during compaction, so the controller exposes a 'freshly written' bit per row and skips refresh on heap regions rewritten within their retention window. Dead regions are never refreshed at all.
why: Cuts refresh operations on managed-heap memory by an estimated 30-70%, with weak-retention rows parked in high-churn nursery spaces.

title: Downhole elastic ECC: parity grows as the die heats
idea: Downhole tools at 200 C trade capacity for survival. Tie on-die ECC strength to a junction-temperature sensor: rows step from a (136,128) SEC code to (144,128) DEC to (160,128) as temperature rises. The extra parity comes from a reserved top-of-memory region that the OS gives up through a memory-balloon driver; when the die is cool, that reserve is usable capacity.
why: Retention halves every ~10 C, so specs written for 95 C over-design cells for the ~95% of time a die spends near 50 C. Elastic redundancy lets cells be specified at typical temperature, roughly a 1.5-2x looser retention spec (fact 3).

title: LPDDR PASR's failure fixed by expiring, poisonable no-refresh memory zones
idea: LPDDR's partial-array self-refresh was rarely used because operating systems could not guarantee which data was disposable. Fix: OS 'ephemeral zones' are never refreshed; allocations there carry a deadline (KV-cache blocks, activations, network buffers), the memory controller poisons any line past its deadline, and the runtime recomputes it (e.g., re-prefill the KV block) on a poisoned read.
why: Zero refresh power for an estimated 30-60% of AI-server memory, with correctness guaranteed by poison semantics instead of stored charge.

title: Unequal protection for KV caches: guard exponents, expose mantissas
idea: Po: memory that forgets the details but keeps the gist. LLM KV-cache tensors are split so sign and exponent bits sit in a strongly coded region while mantissa bits sit raw in 1%-BER cells; softmax averaging turns sparse mantissa flips into a negligible perplexity change.
why: KV cache is a fast-growing share of inference DRAM; ~70% of its bits move to cheap, rarely refreshed cells with ~2% total code overhead.
